# Introduction to the Business Problem

HELP International is an aid organization.

**The problem.** HELP has to decide which countries need its money
most, and it has to explain that choice to its donors.
If you had to rank these 167 countries by need, how would you do it, and
how would you explain your choice to HELP's donors?

The dataset has one observation per country, 167 countries. For each country
we have its name and nine variables: deaths of children under 5, exports,
spending on health, imports, income per person, inflation, life expectancy,
children per woman, and GDP per person. Three are shares of GDP and two are
in dollars per person. The other four are in deaths per 1,000 live births,
percent per year, years, and children per woman. The codebook gives the unit
of each variable. The file does not say which year the data are from.

The question for this lab: how can HELP compare 167 countries on nine
variables at once, in a way it can explain to its donors? How few summary
measures does it need, and what does each one measure? Which countries are
similar? Would HELP send aid in the order this comparison gives, and what
would that order miss?

Keep the case PDF and the
codebook open while you run code.

**Before you run anything.** Suppose HELP lets you keep only one of
the nine variables to rank the countries by need. Which one would you
keep? Name one country that your variable would put in the wrong place,
and say why. Talk this through with the person next to you. We come
back to it in section 8.

# Roadmap

1. **Load the country data and look at the units.** Keep the country name as
   a label. Compare the standard deviations (SDs) of the nine variables.
2. **Run PCA on the variables in their original units.** See which variables
   dominate.
3. **Standardize the variables.** Run PCA again. Read how much of the spread
   (variance) each component explains, the proportion of variance explained
   (PVE), and decide how many components to keep.
4. **Name PC1 from its loadings and the countries at each end.** Fix its
   sign first.
5. **Name PC2 the same way.**
6. **Place every country on the map.** First the biplot, then the map, a
   plot of PC1 against PC2, with the Gulf countries marked.
7. **Check one extreme value before you trust the map:** one country's
   inflation.
8. **Rank the countries and check the list.** Write down how many components
   you keep and your names for PC1 and PC2, then check the ranking of the
   countries on PC1.

We stop there in class. Section 9 has seven more questions to work on after
class.

# 1. Load the country data and look at the units

```{r}
#| label: setup
# This lab uses base R only. There is nothing to install.
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
countries <- read.csv("data/country_data.csv")
# dim() prints the number of countries and the number of variables.
# sum(is.na()) counts missing values in all the data.
dim(countries)
sum(is.na(countries))
# str() shows each variable and its type.
str(countries)

# Question: How many countries are there? Is any value missing? Which
# variable is text?
```

```{r}
#| label: nine-variables
# Why? PCA works only with numeric variables. The country name is text, so
# it stays out of the PCA. We keep it as a label: rownames() attaches the
# names to X, so every table and plot below shows them.
vars <- c("child_mort", "exports", "health", "imports", "income",
          "inflation", "life_expec", "total_fer", "gdpp")
X <- countries[, vars]
rownames(X) <- countries$country
head(X)

# summary() gives the smallest value, the quartiles, the mean and the
# largest value of each variable.
summary(X)

# The SD of each variable, from smallest to largest, and the ratio of the
# largest SD to the smallest.
var_sd <- sapply(X, sd)
round(sort(var_sd), 2)
max(var_sd) / min(var_sd)

# Question: Which two variables have the largest SDs, and what is their
# unit? Which has the smallest SD, and in what unit? Look at the
# codebook: health, exports and imports are shares of GDP. Can a share
# of GDP ever have an SD close to that of income?
```

```{r}
#| label: inflation
# Inflation is the yearly change in prices, in percent. It is most likely
# the change in the GDP deflator, a price index for everything the country
# produces. The file does not say so, and the highest value is far above the
# World Bank figure for that country, so treat this as likely, not certain.
# Below: the five highest values, and the number of countries with inflation
# below zero.
X[order(X$inflation, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], "inflation", drop = FALSE]
sum(X$inflation < 0)

# Question: Which country has the highest inflation? How far is it above the
# second highest? Keep this country in mind. We will come back to it in
# section 7.
```

```{r}
#| label: correlation
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.5
# Why? Before the PCA, look at which variables are correlated. If several
# variables are strongly correlated, one component could summarize them.
# cor() gives the correlation between every two variables. Blue is positive,
# red is negative, and a darker cell is a stronger correlation.
R <- cor(X)
par(mar = c(7, 7, 3, 1))
image(1:9, 1:9, R[, 9:1], zlim = c(-1, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      col = colorRampPalette(c("#C41230", "white", "#1F5FA8"))(100),
      main = "Correlation between every two variables")
axis(1, at = 1:9, labels = vars, las = 2, tick = FALSE)
axis(2, at = 1:9, labels = rev(vars), las = 1, tick = FALSE)
text(rep(1:9, 9), rep(1:9, each = 9), sprintf("%.2f", R[, 9:1]), cex = 0.75)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

# Question: Which variables are strongly correlated with each other? Which
# look unrelated to the rest?
#
# Discuss: If you had to summarize the nine variables with fewer measures,
# which variables would you expect to end up together?
```

# 2. Run PCA on the variables in their original units

```{r}
#| label: pca-raw
# prcomp() always centers each variable: it subtracts the mean. Without
# scale. = TRUE it does not divide by the SD, so each variable keeps its
# original unit. The first row of summary() is the SD of each component, not
# of any variable.
pca_raw <- prcomp(X)
summary(pca_raw)
# The loadings of PC1 and PC2. R stores the loadings in rotation.
round(pca_raw$rotation[, 1:2], 3)

# Question: What share of the spread does PC1 explain? Which two variables
# have loadings on PC1 that are far from zero?
#
# Interpret: In their original units, the variables with the largest spread
# dominate PC1. Name the two variables with large loadings, and give their
# unit.
#
# Question: Find inflation in the loadings. Does Nigeria's extreme
# inflation matter at all in this PCA? Why not?
#
# Discuss: If income were recorded in thousands of dollars instead of
# dollars, would PC1 still be about income? What does that tell you about
# running PCA on variables in their original units?
```

# 3. Standardize the variables

A z-score is (value − mean) / SD. It tells us how many SDs a country is
above or below the mean of all countries. `scale()` turns every variable
into z-scores, so each variable has mean 0 and SD 1.

```{r}
#| label: z-scores
Z <- scale(X)
# Qatar and Nigeria as z-scores. All nine variables are now in the same
# unit, SDs.
round(Z[c("Qatar", "Nigeria"), ], 2)
# Every SD is 1.
round(apply(Z, 2, sd), 2)

# Question: How many SDs above the average is Qatar's income? Nigeria's
# inflation? Which of the two is more extreme?
```

```{r}
#| label: units-vs-sds
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
# The nine variables in their own units (left) and in SDs (right).
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(7, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(X, las = 2, main = "In their own units", cex.axis = 0.8)
boxplot(Z, las = 2, main = "In SDs (z-scores)", cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Interpret: On the left, income and gdpp are so large that the other seven
# variables are hard to see. On the right, all nine are on the same scale.
# Standardizing does not remove extreme values: a country that is extreme in
# its own unit is still extreme as a z-score.
```

```{r}
#| label: pca-scaled
# scale. = TRUE standardizes each variable before running PCA.
pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)

# Why? Each standardized variable has variance 1, so the total variance of
# the nine is 9. The proportion of variance explained (PVE) by a component
# is its variance divided by 9.
pve <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
cum_pve <- cumsum(pve)
round(rbind(PVE = pve, cumulative = cum_pve), 4)

# Question: What is the PVE of PC1 now? Compare it with section 2.
```

```{r}
#| label: scree
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
# Scree plot: the PVE of each component as bars, the cumulative PVE as a
# line, and dashed lines at 80% and 90%.
bars <- barplot(100 * pve, names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:9), ylim = c(0, 100),
                col = "grey80", ylab = "Percent of the spread",
                main = "Share of the spread each component explains")
lines(bars, 100 * cum_pve, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#C41230")
abline(h = c(80, 90), lty = 2, col = "grey40")

# Question: What is the cumulative PVE of PC1 and PC2? How many components
# do you need to pass 80%? And 90%?
#
# Discuss: The map shows only PC1 and PC2. How much of the spread does it
# leave out? To rank countries by need, would HELP be fine with two
# components, or would it need more?
```

# 4. Name PC1 from its loadings and the countries at each end

```{r}
#| label: loadings-r
# The loadings of PC1 and PC2, with the signs R gives.
round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 3)

# Question: Which variables have the largest loadings on PC1, ignoring the
# sign? Which loadings have a minus sign?
#
# Interpret: The sign of a component has no meaning on its own. A set of
# loadings and the same set with every sign flipped describe the same line.
# Flipping the signs of PC1 mirrors the map from left to right. Another
# computer can print the opposite signs for the same data.
```

```{r}
#| label: set-direction
# Why? So that everyone in the room reads the same map. If needed, we flip
# the signs of PC1 so that its loading on life expectancy is positive, and
# the signs of PC2 so that its loading on imports is positive. A flip
# changes the signs of the loadings and of the countries' positions
# together. No distance between two countries changes.
if (pca$rotation["life_expec", "PC1"] < 0) {
  pca$rotation[, "PC1"] <- -pca$rotation[, "PC1"]
  pca$x[, "PC1"] <- -pca$x[, "PC1"]
}
if (pca$rotation["imports", "PC2"] < 0) {
  pca$rotation[, "PC2"] <- -pca$rotation[, "PC2"]
  pca$x[, "PC2"] <- -pca$x[, "PC2"]
}
round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: pc1-loadings
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# The PC1 loadings, sorted: the most positive at the top, the most negative
# at the bottom. Positive loadings are blue, negative are red. The dashed
# lines at -0.33 and 0.33 show the loading each variable would have if all
# nine counted the same.
load_pc1 <- sort(pca$rotation[, "PC1"])
par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 1))
barplot(load_pc1, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, xlim = c(-0.7, 0.7),
        col = ifelse(load_pc1 > 0, "#1F5FA8", "#C41230"),
        xlab = "Loading on PC1", main = "Loadings on PC1")
abline(v = 0)
abline(v = c(-1, 1) / 3, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

# Question: Which variables move a country to the right on PC1? Which move
# it to the left? Which are inside the dashed lines?
```

```{r}
#| label: pc1-ends
# pca$x holds each country's position on each component. The book calls
# these positions the principal component scores. Below: the five countries
# lowest on PC1 and the five highest.
pc1 <- sort(pca$x[, "PC1"])
round(head(pc1, 5), 2)
round(tail(pc1, 5), 2)
# Their values on the nine variables, so you can check your name against the
# data.
X[c(names(head(pc1, 5)), names(tail(pc1, 5))), ]

# Question: Give PC1 a short name a donor would understand. Does your
# name fit both the loadings and the countries at each end?
#
# Discuss: Is the lowest country on PC1 also the lowest in income? In
# life expectancy? How can a country end up lowest on PC1?
```

# 5. Name PC2 the same way

```{r}
#| label: pc2-loadings
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# The PC2 loadings, sorted: the most positive at the top, the most negative
# at the bottom. Positive loadings are blue, negative are red. The dashed
# lines at -0.33 and 0.33 show the loading each variable would have if all
# nine counted the same.
load_pc2 <- sort(pca$rotation[, "PC2"])
par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 1))
barplot(load_pc2, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, xlim = c(-0.7, 0.7),
        col = ifelse(load_pc2 > 0, "#1F5FA8", "#C41230"),
        xlab = "Loading on PC2", main = "Loadings on PC2")
abline(v = 0)
abline(v = c(-1, 1) / 3, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

pc2 <- sort(pca$x[, "PC2"])
round(head(pc2, 5), 2)
round(tail(pc2, 5), 2)
X[c(names(head(pc2, 5)), names(tail(pc2, 5))), c("exports", "imports", "health", "income")]

# Question: Which two variables have the largest loadings on PC2? What do
# the countries at the top have in common? And the countries at the bottom?
#
# Question: Give PC2 a short name. Is PC2 about how rich a country is?
# Check the loading of income.
#
# Discuss: Find one rich country near the top of PC2 and one near the
# bottom. How do their exports and imports compare?
```

# 6. Place every country on the map

```{r}
#| label: biplot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
# A biplot shows the countries and the loadings together. scale = 0 plots
# the positions without rescaling them. The names come from rownames(X).
biplot(pca, scale = 0, cex = c(0.5, 0.8), col = c("grey40", "#C41230"),
       xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")

# Interpret: Each name is a country. Each red arrow is one of the nine
# variables, drawn from its loadings on PC1 and PC2. Countries tend to lie
# in the direction of the arrows of the variables on which they are high.
# With 167 names, the middle of the plot is hard to read.
```

```{r}
#| label: on-map
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# Why? The map shows PC1 and PC2 only. Some variables are shown well on it
# and some are not.
# For each variable, this is the share of its spread that the map shows. The
# factoextra package calls this cos2, the quality of representation. The
# dashed line is the share the map shows for all nine variables together.
on_map <- 100 * rowSums((pca$rotation[, 1:2] %*% diag(pca$sdev[1:2]))^2)
round(sort(on_map), 1)
par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 1))
barplot(sort(on_map), horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "grey60", xlim = c(0, 100),
        xlab = "Share of the variable's spread on the map (%)",
        main = "How well the map shows each variable")
abline(v = 100 * cum_pve[2], lty = 2, col = "#C41230", lwd = 1.5)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

# Question: Which variables does the map show poorly? Find them on the
# biplot above. What do you notice about their arrows?
#
# Discuss: If HELP cares about one of those variables, what should it look
# at besides the map?
```

```{r}
#| label: map
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
# The same positions, with only some countries labeled: the six Gulf
# Cooperation Council (GCC) countries in red, and the countries at the ends
# of PC1 and PC2.
gcc <- c("Bahrain", "Kuwait", "Oman", "Qatar", "Saudi Arabia",
         "United Arab Emirates")
ends <- setdiff(c(names(head(pc1, 4)), names(tail(pc1, 4)),
                  names(head(pc2, 3)), names(tail(pc2, 3))), gcc)
plot(pca$x[, "PC1"], pca$x[, "PC2"], pch = 19, col = "grey75",
     xlim = range(pca$x[, "PC1"]) * 1.15, ylim = range(pca$x[, "PC2"]) * 1.1,
     xlab = paste0("PC1 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pve[1]), "% of the spread)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC2 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pve[2]), "% of the spread)"),
     main = "167 countries on PC1 and PC2")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
# Names go above a point when it is above zero on PC2, below otherwise.
text(pca$x[ends, "PC1"], pca$x[ends, "PC2"], ends,
     pos = ifelse(pca$x[ends, "PC2"] < 0, 1, 3), cex = 0.7)
points(pca$x[gcc, "PC1"], pca$x[gcc, "PC2"], pch = 19, col = "#C41230")
text(pca$x[gcc, "PC1"], pca$x[gcc, "PC2"], gcc, pos = c(4, 4, 2, 4, 1, 4), cex = 0.7, col = "#C41230")

# The positions and ranks of the six Gulf countries. A rank of 1 is the
# highest of the 167.
gcc_table <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[gcc, "PC1"], rank_PC1 = rank(-pca$x[, "PC1"])[gcc],
                        PC2 = pca$x[gcc, "PC2"], rank_PC2 = rank(-pca$x[, "PC2"])[gcc])
round(gcc_table, 2)

# Question: Where is Qatar on PC1 among 167 countries? Are the six Gulf
# countries close together on the map? Which one is farthest from the
# others, and on which component?
#
# Discuss: Qatar has the highest income in the data. Why is it not
# first on PC1?
```

# 7. Check one extreme value before you trust the map

Find the country at the bottom of PC1 and look at its values on the nine
variables. Is it at the bottom because of all nine, or mostly because of
one?

```{r}
#| label: nigeria-contrib
# This is the sum we did by hand for the Plain Bagel on Monday. Multiply
# each loading by the country's z-score on that variable. The result is that
# variable's contribution to the country's position on PC1. Add the nine
# contributions and you get the country's position on PC1. Careful with the
# letters: on Monday, z was the position. Here Z is the matrix of z-scores,
# and the position is pca$x.
contrib <- pca$rotation[, "PC1"] * Z["Nigeria", ]
round(cbind(loading = pca$rotation[, "PC1"], z = Z["Nigeria", ], contribution = contrib), 2)
round(c(sum_of_contrib = sum(contrib), position_PC1 = pca$x["Nigeria", "PC1"]), 2)

# How many countries would sit below Nigeria without its inflation contribution?
sum(pca$x[rownames(X) != "Nigeria", "PC1"] < sum(contrib) - contrib["inflation"])

# Question: Which contribution to PC1 is the largest, ignoring the sign? Is
# it large because of the loading or because of the z-score?
#
# Discuss: Take the inflation contribution out of Nigeria's position. Where
# would Nigeria be on PC1, counting from the bottom? Would you still put it
# first?
```

```{r}
#| label: pc1-share
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# Why? The table above explains one country. This plot is about PC1
# itself, across all 167 countries. A variable's share of PC1 is 100
# times its loading squared. The nine shares add up to 100.
share_pc1 <- 100 * pca$rotation[, "PC1"]^2
round(sort(share_pc1, decreasing = TRUE), 1)
sum(share_pc1)
par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 1))
barplot(sort(share_pc1), horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "grey60",
        xlim = c(0, 20), xlab = "Share of PC1 (%)",
        main = "Each variable's share of PC1")
# The dashed line is 100 / 9 = 11.1%, the share each variable would have
# if all nine counted the same.
abline(v = 100 / 9, lty = 2, col = "#C41230", lwd = 1.5)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

# Note: The factoextra package calls this share the "contribution" of a
# variable, and fviz_contrib() draws this plot. In this lab, contribution
# to PC1 always means loading times z-score for one country, as in the
# table above.
#
# Question: Is inflation above or below the dashed line? Compare that
# with the size of Nigeria's inflation contribution in the table above.
#
# Discuss: To explain why one country sits where it does on PC1, which
# helps more: each variable's share of PC1, or that country's
# contributions? What should HELP check before it trusts one country's
# position?
```

```{r}
#| label: without-nigeria
# The same PCA without Nigeria. Flip the signs the same way as in section 4.
pca_wo <- prcomp(X[rownames(X) != "Nigeria", ], scale. = TRUE)
if (pca_wo$rotation["life_expec", "PC1"] < 0) pca_wo$rotation[, "PC1"] <- -pca_wo$rotation[, "PC1"]
if (pca_wo$rotation["imports", "PC2"] < 0) pca_wo$rotation[, "PC2"] <- -pca_wo$rotation[, "PC2"]
round(cbind(all_PC1 = pca$rotation[, "PC1"], without_PC1 = pca_wo$rotation[, "PC1"],
            all_PC2 = pca$rotation[, "PC2"], without_PC2 = pca_wo$rotation[, "PC2"]), 3)
# The largest change in any loading, on PC1 and on PC2.
loading_change <- apply(abs(pca_wo$rotation[, 1:2] - pca$rotation[, 1:2]), 2, max)
round(loading_change, 3)
pve_wo <- pca_wo$sdev^2 / sum(pca_wo$sdev^2)
round(rbind(all = pve[1:4], without_Nigeria = pve_wo[1:4]), 4)

# Question: Did dropping Nigeria change the loadings of PC1 or PC2? Did the
# PVEs change?
#
# Discuss: The file does not say exactly what this inflation variable
# measures, or for which year. Is Nigeria the country in most need, or the
# country with the most extreme inflation value? What would you check before
# you report to HELP?
```

# 8. Rank the countries and check the list

**Before you decide.** Talk with the person next to you. Look at the scree
plot, your names for PC1 and PC2, and what you found about Nigeria in
section 7. Decide how many components you would keep for HELP, and write a
short name for PC1 and for PC2. Then give your reason in one sentence.
Finally, go back to the one variable you chose at the start to rank the
countries: does it rank them in about the same order as PC1?

```{r}
#| label: commit
# Type the number of components you keep, without quotes. Type the two
# names and your reason between the quotes.
my_k <- NA
pc1_name <- ""
pc2_name <- ""
my_reason <- ""

if (length(my_k) == 1 && is.numeric(my_k) && my_k %in% 1:9) {
  cat("Components kept:", my_k, "\n")
  cat("Share of the spread on the map:", round(cum_pve[my_k], 4), "\n")
  cat("Share left out:", round(1 - cum_pve[my_k], 4), "\n")
  cat("PC1:", pc1_name, "| PC2:", pc2_name, "\n")
  cat("Reason:", my_reason, "\n")
} else {
  cat("No number of components chosen yet. Type a number from 1 to 9 in",
      "my_k, then run this chunk again.\n")
}

# The ten countries lowest on PC1, with their values on the nine variables.
shortlist <- names(pc1)[1:10]
X[shortlist, ]

# Question: Would you send aid in this order? Which country on the
# list would you check first, and with which of the nine variables?
#
# Discuss: PCA uses no outcome variable. Nothing in this dataset says how
# much past aid helped, what aid costs, or who would receive it. What does
# the map not tell HELP?
```

# 9. After class: extra questions

Work on these on your own after class. They use the same data. Run question
1 first, because question 5 uses the distances it computes.

1. **The countries closest to Qatar.** Find the five countries nearest to
   Qatar on the map (PC1 and PC2), and the five nearest on all nine
   standardized variables. Are they the same countries? What does the map
   hide about Qatar?

2. **What PC3 and PC4 add.** Use your scree plot from section 3. Read the
   loadings of PC3 and PC4 and the countries at each end. Where is Nigeria
   on PC3? Compare the PC3 loadings with and without Nigeria. Do they change
   more than the PC1 and PC2 loadings did in section 7?

3. **Is it only the dollar variables?** Run PCA on the variables in their
   original units, leaving out income and gdpp. Which variable dominates PC1
   now, and why?

4. **The shortlist without inflation.** Run the PCA on the eight
   standardized variables other than inflation. Where does Nigeria rank on
   PC1 now? How many of the ten countries are on both shortlists?

5. **Close on the map, close in the data?** Among pairs of countries less
   than 0.1 apart on the map, find the pair that is farthest apart on all
   nine standardized variables. Compare their values. How far apart are
   they, compared with the median distance between two countries?

6. **The correlations and PC1.** Look back at the correlation heatmap
   from section 1. Are the variables that are strongly correlated with
   each other the ones with the largest loadings on PC1?

7. **Drop every extreme value?** A common rule drops any observation
   with a z-score above 3 or below -3 on any variable. How many countries
   does the rule drop? How many of them are on your shortlist from
   section 8? Run the PCA without them. Does PC1 change? Would you use
   this rule for HELP?

```{r}
#| label: after-class-qatar
#| eval: false
# After class, change eval to true. Do not run these in class.
# dist() gives the straight-line (Euclidean) distance between every pair of
# countries: on the map (PC1 and PC2), and on the nine standardized
# variables.
d_map <- as.matrix(dist(pca$x[, c("PC1", "PC2")]))
d_all <- as.matrix(dist(Z))
near_map <- names(sort(d_map["Qatar", ]))[2:6]
near_all <- names(sort(d_all["Qatar", ]))[2:6]
near_map
near_all
round(rbind(map = d_map["Qatar", near_map], all_nine = d_all["Qatar", near_map]), 2)
X[unique(c("Qatar", near_map, near_all)), ]
```

```{r}
#| label: after-class-pc3-pc4
#| eval: false
# After class, change eval to true. Do not run these in class.
# Same rule as in section 4: flip PC3 so its loading on health is positive,
# and PC4 so its loading on gdpp is positive.
if (pca$rotation["health", "PC3"] < 0) {
  pca$rotation[, "PC3"] <- -pca$rotation[, "PC3"]
  pca$x[, "PC3"] <- -pca$x[, "PC3"]
}
if (pca$rotation["gdpp", "PC4"] < 0) {
  pca$rotation[, "PC4"] <- -pca$rotation[, "PC4"]
  pca$x[, "PC4"] <- -pca$x[, "PC4"]
}
round(pca$rotation[, 3:4], 3)
round(head(sort(pca$x[, "PC3"]), 4), 2)
round(tail(sort(pca$x[, "PC3"]), 4), 2)
round(head(sort(pca$x[, "PC4"]), 4), 2)
round(tail(sort(pca$x[, "PC4"]), 4), 2)
round(pca$x["Nigeria", 1:4], 2)
if (pca_wo$rotation["health", "PC3"] < 0) pca_wo$rotation[, "PC3"] <- -pca_wo$rotation[, "PC3"]
round(cbind(all_PC3 = pca$rotation[, "PC3"], without_PC3 = pca_wo$rotation[, "PC3"]), 3)
round(max(abs(pca_wo$rotation[, "PC3"] - pca$rotation[, "PC3"])), 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: after-class-three-sds
#| eval: false
# After class, change eval to true. Do not run these in class.
# TRUE for a country with any z-score above 3 or below -3.
extreme <- rowSums(abs(Z) > 3) > 0
sum(extreme)
names(which(extreme))
intersect(shortlist, names(which(extreme)))
# The same PCA without them. Flip the sign of PC1 the same way as in section 4.
pca_trim <- prcomp(X[!extreme, ], scale. = TRUE)
if (pca_trim$rotation["life_expec", "PC1"] < 0) {
  pca_trim$rotation[, "PC1"] <- -pca_trim$rotation[, "PC1"]
  pca_trim$x[, "PC1"] <- -pca_trim$x[, "PC1"]
}
round(cbind(all = pca$rotation[, "PC1"], trimmed = pca_trim$rotation[, "PC1"]), 3)
pve_trim <- pca_trim$sdev^2 / sum(pca_trim$sdev^2)
round(rbind(all = pve[1:4], trimmed = pve_trim[1:4]), 4)
```
